entities.name: Smithsonian Institution
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Smithsonian Institution, founded in 1846 through a bequest of £104,960 from British scientist James Smithson (who never visited America) to create 'an establishment for the increase and diffusion of knowledge,' is the world's largest museum complex — encompassing 19 museums, 21 libraries, 9 research centers, and over 154 million artifacts and specimens. The Smithsonian's free-admission National Mall museums in Washington D.C. receive 22 million visitors annually, making it the most visited museum complex on earth.

James Smithson, an illegitimate son of the Duke of Northumberland who achieved scientific distinction without social recognition, bequeathed his estate to a country he had never visited — apparently motivated by a desire to spite the English aristocracy that had excluded him. The 1836 bequest and the 8-year American congressional debate about accepting it (many saw it as inappropriate for a republic to accept money from a foreign aristocrat) eventually created the 'National Attic' of American civilization under first Secretary Joseph Henry.

The Smithsonian's collections span from the Hope Diamond (at the Natural History Museum) and the Wright Brothers' 1903 Flyer (at Air and Space) to the original Star-Spangled Banner flag and the first McDonald's french fry machine. The Institution runs the world's largest biological specimen collection (145 million), publishes the Smithsonian Magazine (3 million subscribers), and operates research stations from the Amazon to the Arctic. The Smithsonian's free admission policy — funded by the federal government — embodies a democratic commitment to public education unique among world-class museums.
